Dreadful first 30 minutes from Liverpool but they have woken up since, and now they are strong favourites to win the game from here. Iraola’s selection gamble backfired somewhat, but he may well get away with it.

From the second phase of a corner, Ngumoha did well to keep the ball alive and lift a cross to the back post. Cardona tried to usher the ball behind and made the fatal mistake of letting it bounce in his penalty area, and Araujo sneaked in to score from close range.

The goalscorer Cardona makes a mistake to let Ngumoha’s cross drift to the backpost. That’s Liverpool’s equaliser from Ronald Araujo. As soon as Liverpool have got their act together they have looked dangerous.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

The crowd were impatient with him early in the half, but Gakpo is looking more of a threat now, Cruyff-turning away and shooting in the box but Veiga was across to block. Just the one minute of added time to play.

Gakpo wins Liverpool a free-kick in a shooting position left of centre, tripped after Nyoni had carried the ball well through midfield. Too much air on the attempt from Mac Allister, who a couple of minutes earlier fired not too far wide from 25 yards.

Plenty for Andoni Iraola to be annoyed about, but as a spectacle this has been far more entertaining than initially assumed.

Really slick interplay from Villarreal again, and Moleiro’s shot from 25 yards is pushed over the bar by Alisson. You can pick holes in Liverpool, but Villarreal’s play deserves plaudits too.

Alexis Mac Allister grabs a goal back for Liverpool 🔴 Game 🔛 https://t.co/Ml9OYgbNq6

Liverpool have scarcely merited a goal but they have one via a set-piece. Alexis Mac Allister was up early at the near post and he produced a well-directed glancing header into the far corner. That changes the complexion of the game.

Great finish from Mac Allister. The opportunity for Gakpo to cross from the left - that won the corner - was made by Koumas’ hold-up play. First time he has really got hold of it and pinned the defender.

Another run from deep causes Liverpool’s defence problems, but Mikautadze took a touch when a first-time pass could have released the runner through on goal. More groans from the crowd when Tsimikas is caught on the ball.

Then Gakpo flashes a better ball across the face of goal, and Veiga glances it behind for a Liverpool corner.

Villarreal want a corner, and they should have one after a shot deflects off Araujo’s back. Goal kick given though.

Gakpo and Koumas are on the wrong wavelength, and there are groans from the crowd at another misplaced pass.

Liverpool need to dig themselves out of a hole now, Villarreal have cut them apart to score a simple second. Cardona, the left-back, with a run from deep, and Tsimikas was playing him onside. Cardona had all the time in the world to steady himself and roll the ball beyond Alisson.

Defensive calamity for Liverpool. Both Mikautadze and Cardona could have taken that through ball from Saliba and finished.

Straight through the heart of the defence 👀 Sergi Cardona doubles Villarreal's lead at Anfield 🤯 https://t.co/ZPHAkiLjN0

Liverpool far too easy to play through at the moment, Villarreal might not be an elite team but they have enough technique to pass and move well if given the time. Mikautadze lacks some pace up front, but has shown some silky touches. As Alan Shearer puts in on Amazon Prime: “Feels like a training match for Liverpool. So lazy. Where’s the urgency?”

Better from Liverpool with Nyoni driving forward and the ball almost running into the path of Gravenberch for a strike from the edge of the box. Villarreal diligent in their defensive work though, no clear sight of goal for the Liverpool players so far.

Anyone who is experiencing Anfield on a European night for the first time will be wondering what all the fuss is about. Aside from a couple of flurries following a Ronald Araujo tackle and a Rio Ngumoha dribble, it has been deathly quiet. Rafael Benitez, an architect of some of the wildest evenings here, is in the press box alongside Robbie Fowler and they are a reminder of how it used to be. Liverpool need to raise themselves to bring the crowd to life.

Ngumoha is the one ray of light for Liverpool so far, he has the beating of Villarreal left-back Cardona whenever he drops a shoulder. Gulasci palms his deflected cross over and Villarreal survive the corner.

The flag was eventually raised for offside, but Villarreal were in behind the Liverpool defence again after a misplaced Van Dijk pass. Liverpool have not got themselves out of the blocks at all. They have lost possession too cheaply and look vulnerable defensively.

Buchanan with a teasing low cross through the Liverpool penalty area, and the winger is justified when looking quizzically at his team-mates. If one of the yellow shirts had gambled they would have had a tap in.

Most of Liverpool’s attacks are being funnelled down their right so far, perhaps no surprise given that is where Ngumoha is stationed. Liverpool yet to test the goalkeeper, though.

Villarreal then throw a punch of their own down the other end, with Saliba turning and shooting at the edge of the box. Deflected, and Villarreal have a corner. Delivery is poor and Liverpool clear.

The Spanish team are moving the ball around with assurance, some nice touches from Saliba in their midfield (the Canada international is no relation to the Arsenal centre-back).

Hats off to Villarreal coach Inigo Perez, who is not wearing a hat or, indeed, a coat. Instead he is steadfastly ignoring the cold drizzle and treating this, from a touchline outfit point of view, like a warm summer’s evening on the Valencian coast. Polo shirt and slacks for the young Spanish coach.

No need for Liverpool to panic just yet, plenty of time to turn this around, and Rio Ngumoha is going the right way about it. Quick feet in the box to beat his man and fashion a yard for a strike, but his shot is blocked. Ngumoha is playing on Liverpool’s right tonight with Gakpo on the opposite flank.

What a remarkable start. Virgil van Dijk has looked a gear or two behind everyone in the opening stages. One bad touch required Jeremy Jacquet to make a swift recovery and that misplaced header has now handed Villarreal the lead. Social media will be abuzz with scrutiny about Van Dijk now, as is always the case when he errs, but it won’t be taken into consideration that he has been one of Liverpool’s best players in these opening 10 games. What price would you make him to atone with a header at the other end later in the game?

Van Dijk has made two dreadful mistakes in the first four minutes and this time he is punished. Liverpool’s captain was trying to guide a header back to Alisson, but the ball shanked off his forehead at the wrong angle and dropped for Mikautadze in the box. The striker was free, and he finished well across Alisson. That was not in the script.

The Georgian No 9 for Villarreal Georges Mikautadze had looked so lightweight in the early duels with Virgil Van Dijk and Jeremy Jacquet. They had muscled him off the ball more than once. That was a gift from Van Dijk and Mikautadze took it very well.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa

Ryan Gravenberch has started the game in a more advanced midfield role with Nyoni and Mac Allister behind him. The home team are yet to string together a serious sequence of passes in the Villarreal half.

Liverpool trying to harry their opponents early on, but Van Dijk makes a hash of dealing with a simple long ball forward. Villarreal’s striker Mikautadze took too long to bring the ball down and the chance was gone with Jacquet closing him out.

It’s another young Liverpool team fielded in the Champions League, but they should have enough about them to see off this Villarreal side.

Out to get warm! ♨️ https://t.co/75qTJA6L42

We have two important wins for us but we cannot stop. A very good team in front of us and I hope we are at the level of the game.

Different circumstances. It’s out fourth game in 10 days, Florian [Wirtz] and Bradley [Barcola] have played almost every minute so we have to be sensible and the same with Alex [Isak].

I think he is doing very well [Leiws Koumas], or else we would not trust him to start these kinds of games.

Probably difficult to find someone who knows me better [than Inigo Perez], but we also know him!

Villarreal XI: Gulacsi, Mourino, Navarro, Veiga, Cardona, Saliba, Gueye, Buchanan, Comesana, Moleiro, Mikautadze

Subs: Junior, Costa, Freeman, Diatta, Gerard, Foyth, Akhomach, Macia, Oluwaseyi, Perez, El Jmili, Gaitan Diaz

Liverpool XI: Alisson; Araujo, Jacquet, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; Gravenberch, Nyoni, Mac Allister; Ngumoha, Koumas, Gakpo

Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Kerkez, Wirtz, Isak, Barcola, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Laffey

A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

#1285. Serie A | Inter 2-0 Como: Fabregas cannot crack Chivu code

Inter continued their remarkable record against Como, as Francesco Pio Esposito and Marcus Thuram brought Cesc Fabregas back down to earth after nine Champions League goals.

This was a fascinating Scudetto fight and local derby, but with very different moods. The Nerazzurri suffered their first Serie A defeat of the season in the Derby della Madonnina with Milan, but then crushed Feyenoord 3-0 in the Champions League midweek. Como made history with Wednesday’s 9-1 victory away to RC Lens, their sixth straight win in all competition.

Lautaro Martinez and Luis Henrique were still out of action, but John Stones and Curtis Jones were back on the bench after several weeks. Moise Kean, Trevoh Chalobah, Assane Diao, Jesus Rodriguez and Jayden Addai didn’t make the trip.

The breakthrough came when Federico Dimarco robbed Lucas Da Cunha to spark the counter-attack, Marcus Thuram’s smart disguised pass sent Djed Spence down the right to roll across for the Pio Esposito tap-in from a couple of yards.

#1284. Six highlights from Parkinson’s disease research

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Nuwer is a freelance writer based in New York City.

Personalized deep-brain stimulation improved the gait mechanics of people with Parkinson’s disease.Credit: K. H. Louie et al. Nature Med. 32, 2803–2814 (2026)

Deep-brain stimulation (DBS), in which electrodes are implanted in the brain to reduce the symptoms of certain neurological disorders, is often used to treat motor symptoms of Parkinson’s disease. But DBS does not usually improve gait, in part because it delivers a continuous current of electricity that does not account for the shifting demands of walking.

Researchers at the University of California, San Francisco, tested a DBS approach that adjusts stimulation during different phases of the gait cycle. Using neurostimulators implanted in five participants, the team recorded brain activity and delivered electrical stimulation as the individuals walked. The researchers analysed the brain-activity data to identify a personalized neural signature for the leg-swing phases of each participant. This was used to programme the device to recognize brain-activity patterns during walking, and to adjust stimulation automatically at specific phases of the gait cycle.

The researchers confirmed that the gait-synchronized stimulation improved the participants’ step symmetry and reduced the variability of their steps, compared with conventional continuous stimulation. Three participants also completed a multi-day trial at home, in which synchronized stimulation improved their gait mechanics in different ways. One person’s steps became significantly more even in length, for example; another person reported fewer falls.

The technique has at least one drawback: participants tended to report worse stiffness under synchronized rather than continuous stimulation. Still, according to the authors, the study demonstrates that DBS can be synchronized to walking dynamics, opening the door to more-personalized stimulation strategies for gait dysfunction.

Clumps of misfolded α-synuclein protein are a hallmark of Parkinson’s disease, yet there is still no way to image the pathological protein reliably in a live brain. This is in contrast to Alzheimer’s disease, for which diagnosis has been improved using specific tracers of amyloid and tau proteins in positron emission tomography (PET). The tracers bind to those proteins and carry a radioactive tag for imaging.

A team led by researchers at the University of Tübingen in Germany has now developed a PET system to trace α-synuclein. In laboratory tests, the tracer not only bound to α-synuclein with high affinity, but was also more selective for the protein than for other types of aggregate. In rodents and monkeys, the tracer entered the brain readily and cleared quickly.

In a first step towards human trials, the team gave the tracer to four people: one with Parkinson’s, two with multiple system atrophy (another condition characterized by α-synuclein accumulation) and one healthy volunteer. In the participants with diagnoses, the tracer generated signals in the brain regions expected to have α-synuclein pathology; in the healthy volunteer, it produced only a faint signal. The authors conclude that the PET technique is a promising way to image α-synuclein in the living brain.

The prevalence of Parkinson’s disease is rising worldwide, but researchers have struggled to understand whether this is being driven by ageing populations, by more people surviving after diagnosis or because more people are developing the disease. Scientists at Sorbonne University in Paris and the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm used national health registers of the entire populations of their countries to track the prevalence of Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and motor neuron disease over two decades.

The researchers found that the prevalence of all three conditions has risen steadily over time, but that the underlying drivers differed. For Parkinson’s, the number of new diagnoses each year stayed flat and, once adjusted for population ageing, declined slightly. This suggests that the rate of people developing the disease is not increasing. Although survival times had been getting longer, the trend was not sustained over the past ten years.

These findings are in contrast to those for the two other diseases. For multiple sclerosis, rising prevalence was driven mainly by improved survival, probably because of disease-modifying drugs, whereas the rise in prevalence of motor neuron disease seems to reflect an increase in cases. The researchers point out that their findings come from high-income countries with universal health care, so might not generalize to other places.

Scientists have long associated Parkinson’s disease with brain regions that control movement in specific body parts. Researchers at the Changping Laboratory in Beijing instead propose that Parkinson’s is a disorder of the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN), which coordinates whole-body action.

The researchers pooled brain scans from 863 people — including healthy volunteers as well as people with Parkinson’s and other movement disorders — and compared how their brain regions are wired together. They found that the people with Parkinson’s had excessive connectivity between deep-brain structures and the SCAN, and that the strength of those connections correlated with symptom severity. The team also showed that several of the most effective interventions for Parkinson’s — including transcranial magnetic stimulation — reduce SCAN hyperconnectivity.

In a randomized experiment, the authors assigned 36 people with Parkinson’s to receive two weeks of transcranial magnetic stimulation aimed either at the SCAN or at motor regions. Compared with conventional stimulation, SCAN-targeted stimulation roughly doubled the reduction in overall motor symptoms, including improving issues related to tremors, muscle rigidity and speed of movement. The authors propose that SCAN hyperconnectivity could be used as a diagnostic marker for Parkinson’s and that SCAN-targeted treatments could enhance patient outcomes.

Air pollution is a recognized risk factor for dementia, but its specific role in two related conditions — dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson’s disease with dementia — has been unclear. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, combined large-scale human data with mouse and cell experiments to show that particulate matter smaller than 2.5 micrometres in diameter (PM2.5) promotes abnormal aggregation of a protein called α-synuclein, which forms the Lewy bodies that underlie these dementias.

Data from more than 56 million users of the US federal health-insurance system Medicare suggested that long-term PM2.5 exposure was associated with a risk of hospitalization for disorders that involve α-synuclein. This link was stronger for the two dementia diagnoses than for Parkinson’s without dementia. The researchers also showed that, in mice, chronic exposure to air pollution caused brain shrinkage and cognitive decline. Mice engineered to lack α-synuclein were protected from these effects, suggesting that the protein has a causative role.

Finally, the authors showed that PM2.5 from sources in China, the United States and Europe all caused α-synuclein to misfold into a more aggressive strain that spread faster between cells and was more toxic to neurons than were ordinary clumps of the protein. Injecting this strain into mice caused mainly cognitive rather than motor deficits. The authors propose that pollution-induced α-synuclein is an environmentally triggered mechanism contributing to Lewy body dementia.

Scientists are increasingly viewing Parkinson’s disease as two subtypes on the basis of where the disease originates: the brain or the body, particularly the gut. People with these subtypes have different initial symptoms that eventually converge when misfolded aggregates of the protein α-synuclein spread. Although imaging data support the existence of these subtypes, scientists have struggled to collect pathological evidence of where the protein aggregates and how it spreads.

To investigate, researchers at Zhengzhou University in China turned to the skin for its high density of nerves and ease of sampling. They recruited 205 people with Parkinson’s and 60 healthy people. The researchers sorted the Parkinson’s group into the two subtypes according to whether the participants had experienced a disorder of rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep — a typical marker of body-first Parkinson’s — before developing motor symptoms. They took skin biopsies from the lower leg and the back of the neck of each participant and analysed the samples for α-synuclein.

The results revealed differences between the groups. Those with a body-first pattern of disease had significantly more misfolded α-synuclein than did those in the brain-first group: 92% compared with 62%. In the body-first group, the abnormal protein was detected more often in the leg, whereas the brain-first group had slightly higher rates in the neck than in the leg — observations that are consistent with where each subtype begins. The body-first participants also had α-synuclein that clumped faster in laboratory tests.

The differences support the two-subtype model, the authors say, and suggest that skin biopsies could be a minimally invasive tool that helps to classify people according to their disease subtype.

#1283. He's Wanted: Man Utd May Have Another JJ Gabriel Situation as 17 y/o Yet to Sign Deal

Manchester United could have another JJ Gabriel situation on their hands, with another youngster yet to sign a new contract at Old Trafford, and he's attracting plenty of interest.

GIVEMESPORT understands that Gabriel is closing in on a move to Spanish giants Real Madrid after he previously made it clear that he wanted to have his registration terminated in order to leave the club.

Gabriel has been linked with almost every big club around Europe, but it appears that Madrid are close to winning the race for his signature.

United will be entitled to some compensation when it comes to Gabriel's departure, but it's certainly going to be minimal in comparison to the sort of fee they'd want for a player of his potential.

Unfortunately for United and many clubs, they are always left in difficult situations when it comes to young talents without professional contracts, and the Red Devils could have a similar situation with another one of their youngsters.

According to a report from Telegraph journalist Mike McGrath, Manchester United youngster Jariyah Shah is the latest academy product to be attracting interest from around Europe.

The 17-year-old talent has been watched by Juventus, Monaco, Sturm Graz, and Dutch clubs, and he too could move for a small fee due to the fact that he's yet to sign a professional contract with the Red Devils.

Unlike Gabriel, Shah hasn't indicated that he's unsettled, but with a host of different clubs showing an interest in him, there's every chance he follows in the footsteps of the Real Madrid-bound teenager.

It's believed that United are expected to offer professional terms to Shah, but he's set to play at the U17 World Cup, where even more clubs will likely be keeping a close eye on him if he performs.

Man Utd are eyeing a move for a new left-back target in January after an intense scouting mission.

Shah was born in and represents Australia at international youth level, and he made the move to United a few years ago.

He joined the club at U13 level and signed scholarship terms with United back in 2025. Shah joined United from Doncaster Rovers and made his U18 league debut in February 2025.

Shah has played nine times for United's U18 side in the U18 Premier League so far this season, scoring twice and providing an assist.

Shah is eligible to represent England, Australia, Pakistan, and Vietnam, but has only represented Australia at youth level so far in his career.

Of course, losing Shah wouldn't appear to be as big a blow as Gabriel, but he's clearly a highly rated talent given the number of clubs keeping a close eye on his development.

#1282. Leeds defender Jayden Bogle victim of racial abuse online after escaping red card for challenge on Tottenham's Mathys Tel

Published: 14:00 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 14:02 EDT, 8 November 2026

Jayden Bogle has been racially abused online after Leeds’ Premier League win over Tottenham on Saturday.

His club have promised to push for ‘the strongest possible action’ if those responsible for the posts can be identified.

Leeds’ statement read: ‘Leeds United are appalled at the disgusting, racist social media abuse Jayden Bogle suffered following Saturday’s Premier League victory against Tottenham Hotspur.

‘Leeds United condemns this behaviour in the strongest possible terms. There is no place for racism in football or society.

‘The club will work with the Premier League and relevant authorities to identify the individuals and push for the strongest possible action to be taken against them.

‘Jayden has the full and unconditional support of the club and his team-mates, and we all stand with him at this time. Nobody should ever be subjected to racist abuse.’

Jayden Bogle has been the victim of sickening racial abuse after avoiding a red card for this challenge against Tottenham on Saturday

Leeds have promised to push for legal action to be taken against the abusers if they can be identified

Along with the racist and highly offensive messages, the posts, believed to have come from four separate accounts, featured emojis of monkeys and bananas.

Bogle was involved in a controversial incident during the Tottenham game. The 26-year-old escaped a red card when his studs made heavy contact with the ankle of Mathys Tel, forcing the Spurs player to go off injured.

After the game, Leeds boss Daniel Farke said: ‘Jayden is one of the fairest players in the country.

He is more like a butterfly than an eagle and he would not even foul a player on purpose, let alone injure them. It was never intentional and maybe this is why the VAR said it was not a red card.’

#1281. Carrick apology to United fans ominously similar to Solskjaer’s final match

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

And that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

In that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

"I think sometimes we have to be more brave under pressure." Captain Bruno Fernandes gives his immediate reaction to Manchester United's heavy 4-1 defeat to Como 🗣️ 🎙️ @LiamMacdevitt 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/8bzmLGkRAX

There may be some truth in that, but Carrick’s response felt the most accurate assessment of the lot and will certainly chime with supporters who have long questioned how and why so many United sides, regardless of the manager, reach a point where running, intensity and urgency seem optional. “Whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win,” Carrick said.

Carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. He even described Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds as a “fresh start”. But Como blew the lid off any pretence of that being the case. Even by the standards of this season to date, though, what unfolded here in the rain in Lombardy was shocking to witness.

Como, inspired by the outstanding Nico Paz, were every bit as good as United – who have won just two of 11 games this season – were a pitiful mess.

Having conceded after just 47 seconds to Atlético Madrid last week, United were behind after only 118 seconds this time. That in itself told you a lot about these players and this team and it set the tone for what was to follow: a masterclass in incompetence and indifference. There have only been four worse results in United’s European history, although you will struggle to find a poorer performance than this.

Paz scored the first and third goals and set up a wondrous second for Tasos Douvikas that showcased Como’s talent at the same time as underlining United’s myriad fault lines. Paz was just unplayable for much of an evening when United never got close to getting to grips with the young Argentine, whose big physique belies a bewitching ability on the ball. United, by contrast, were a sorry collection of strangers. It was impossible to discern a game plan. United were sent out in a strange 4-2-4, with Fernandes and Youri Tielemans operating as almost double false nines. Glenn Hoddle said on TNT Sports that it was like United were “playing in chains”.

Neither looked sure of what they were supposed to be doing. There was just a giant hole where the attack should have been. Everything about them was slow, leaden. The confusion was contagious. Everywhere you looked there were players second-guessing themselves, uncertain of their role and position and habitually a yard or two or three off the pace. But was there any excuse for not running, for so little effort?

The space Paz was afforded to curl in a fine finish less than two minutes in was alarming in the extreme. Carrick brought on Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo for the lamentable Mateus Cunha and Andrey Santos at half-time, but United just got worse.

There was not so much as a snip at the heels of the same player when Paz ghosted in from the right flank, running 30 yards deep into the penalty area before again finishing coolly for the third. Ramón had a free header for the fourth.

As for that second shortly after the restart? First the impressive Lucas Da Cunha rolled Baleba too easily. Noussair Mazraoui got sucked in trying to mark Martin Baturina in the middle, but got nowhere close as the Como winger played a lovely first-time pass in behind for Paz, who had run off the back of Mason Mount. Douvikas had positioned himself on Matthijs de Ligt’s blind side and the defender, making his first appearance for 11 months, had no idea where the Greece striker was before he darted across the front of him to receive Paz’s pass and dink the ball over Senne Lammens.

For Como, who were playing in Italy’s third tier five years ago, this was one of the greatest nights in their history. For United, it was one of the worst. Carrick may pay a heavy price for it, but there are far greater problems than the manager at this football club.

United enjoy a spell inside the attacking third to close the half, but it’s too late, at least for the first 45 minutes. The referee blows his whistle and we reach half-time with Como a goal to the good.

There are boos at half-time from United’s travelling support.

United send both of their full-backs forward and it gives Cunha the space to get a shot away from just outside of the box, but his curled effort sails over.

There will be one minute of time added on at the end of this half.

That’s a let off for United. Yan Couto, one of two former Manchester City signings in the Como team, carves open the United defence with a lovely pass and Douvikas should have done better with the finish.

Amazing the difference when you have a centre forward prepared to run in behind. Who would have thought it?

Baturina is the latest to threaten Lammens’ goal. His strike from the edge of the box stings the Belgian’s gloves and Douvikas, who attempts to latch on to the rebound, is offside.

Penalty shout for Como! Douvikas is sent through and it looks as though Lammens is in trouble as he sticks out a leg over which the Greek tumbles, but replays show Lammens withdraws his outstretched limb in the nick of time.

There was also an offside in the build-up, so it does not matter anyway.

Milla and Perrone are really pulling the strings in Como’s midfield. The former comes from the Jose Bordalas/Getafe school of football (think Tony Pulis during peak Britannia era) but you would not guess it given the way he manipulates the ball.

This game has entered into something of a holding pattern, with Como retaining possession as United chase shadows, desperately trying to lock off the centre of the park.

Here, Coute inverts, picking up the ball in the inside right channels before spinning in a ball over the top for Douvikas to stride on to, but the Greece forward shanks his shot over the bar.

Thirty four minutes in and the first chants of “attack, attack, attack” can be heard from the United fans. There is currently a giant hole where you would expect United’s strikers to be. It’s so poor.

Lammens does well to get down smartly and keep out a Douvikas effort, speared towards the near post after a sweeping counter attack. The resulting corner fails to threaten United’s defensive unit.

Da Cunha, fresh off his first France call-up, has just sold Mazraoui a dream, spinning the Moroccan in the middle of the pitch before gliding upfield, sweeping the ball out to Valle on the left, whose cross is far too loopy to trouble Lammens.

For seemingly the first time in this match, one of United’s full-backs, Mazraoui, makes a darting run in behind. While the ball goes through to the goalkeeper, it’s the right sort of intent.

Paz escapes the vicious clutches of Santos, but bumps into Cunha’s outstretched leg and earns a foul near the halfway line. Santos, already on a yellow, will need to careful not to get caught doing anything untoward for the remaining 60 minutes of this match.

It’s hard to detect a game plan from United. Como look like they know what what they’ve been told to do but United are just all over the place. Andrey Santos will be grateful referee Sven Jablonski was lenient the first time he came through the back of Paz because he’s just scythed through him a second time minutes later and picked up a yellow.

That’s better from United. Cunha hits the by-line aggressively but his cross is cut out.

Paz then breaks away down the right and, sensing a lack of cover, Santos dives in and receives a yellow card for his troubles.

United string together perhaps their best sequence of the match, shifting the ball quickly from one side to the other, with Mount and Cunha combining, but the move breaks down when Tielemans’ attempted through-ball is cut out by Kempf.

Fernandes attempts to play in Tielemans between the lines but his pass is behind the Belgian and Como regain possession. It’s rinse and repeat moments later, but on the far side.

The detail on United’s passes has been so poor thus far, with Como picking up loose balls all over the pitch.

Penalty shout for Como! Da Cunha, Douvikas and Baturina combine expertly through the middle, trading the ball with cultured one-touch passes. Baturina is felled by Maguire inside United’s box just as he was gearing up to shoot, but neither the referee nor the VAR are minded to intervene. There is a touch, but it does seem very slight.

United have gone with the box midfield once more, with Fernandes rolling inside as a false 9. Como are counteracting United’s movements through Paz dropping in, so Carrick’s men are struggling to take control of the central zones.

Mbeumo bursts towards the by-line but Ramon gets back sharply to divert the ball behind for a corner, which is easily dealt with.

United drop into a deep block, forcing Como to build around the outside. The ball is worked to the adventurous Couto who loses his boot after an overzealous challenge from Cunha and he earns a free-kick for his troubles, but Da Cunha’s delivery fails to beat the first man.

Chance! Da Cunha plays a lovely through-ball into the right channel for Paz to gallop on to and he flashes the ball across the face of goal, but Maguire gets there before Douvikas and the ball is cleared.

United are struggling to string passes together as Paz cuts out a Lammens pass out from the back, but he cannot keep the ball in play.

United need to settle, and here they decide it best to keep hold of the ball for a while. There are a few sideways passes but the ball goes back to Como.

Valle makes a burst down the left and Dalot’s contact results in a foul, but the free-kick is not up to much.

Como 1 Manchester United 0 (Paz) Well, we said he was special! Como work the ball out to the right, with Da Cunha picking out Paz on the edge of the box. Neither of United’s centre-halves are minded to close the Argentine down, and he opens up his body before shaping the ball around Lammens and inside the far post. Golazo.

Harry Amass has been a feature on United’s bench this season and some thought the 19-year-old could become Carrick’s sixth left-back of the season, but it looks as though Mazraoui will play there tonight.

Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick said he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick said before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

#1280. Vanoli: ‘Fiorentina need experience and balance’ against rivals Juventus

Paolo Vanoli explains some of his unexpected Fiorentina picks against Juventus, insisting they need ‘experience’ to control this very important fixture.

It kicks off at the Stadio Artemio Franchi at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from today’s five Serie A games on the Liveblog.

This is never a regular fixture due to the bitter history between the two clubs, which is why the Viola are so pleased with their recent results against their rivals.

They are unbeaten against Juventus since April 2024, managing two wins and as many stalemates.

“I experienced this game as a player and a coach, I always tried to explain to the players what it means to wear this jersey, especially in a fixture like this,” Vanoli told DAZN Italia.

“We need to represent it proudly in every game, above all one like this where we can write history.”

Pedro Goncalves is a surprising pick, while Christ Inao Oulai is another unexpected starter instead of ex-Juventus midfielder Niccolò Fagioli.

“When I talk about balance, it also means mental strength. Goncalves is accustomed to this type of pressure, so I hope his experience can help him to handle the role. However, the most important thing the whole team needs is courage.

“A player cannot be 100 per cent in every game, sometimes he needs a breather to recapture his sharpness. Oulai deserved an opportunity, he had very different characteristics, but I would say neither Oulai nor Fagioli are traditional playmakers,” explained Vanoli.

“We are a team built to keep the ball and I like to defend with the ball at our feet, whereas sometimes we get a little over-excited and try to attack at all times.”

Fiorentina have had another chaotic campaign, as Fabio Grosso was sacked on September 6 after just four competitive games, bringing Paolo Vanoli back to the Stadio Franchi.

This initially brought a boost, then two points from five rounds until Monday’s 4-2 success away to troubled Sassuolo.

#1279. South Korean star Kim Min-su has no goals and no assists, but it's no problem for Rangers boss Derek McInnes

Published: 14:24 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 14:24 EDT, 8 November 2026

Kim Min-su’s stat sheet since making the big-money move to Rangers over the summer should be the kind of thing that makes a manager legitimately wonder if both he and the club have been taken for a ride.

Twelve games, zero goals, zero assists. A rank-rotten return, on the face of it. So why does Derek McInnes not seem even remotely concerned by the whole palaver?

Well, simply put, he has a set of eyes. He, like everyone else, can clearly see that the South Korean is the heartbeat of everything that has been good about Rangers in an attacking sense ever since he was thrown into the team – even if the numbers don’t quite back it up.

It was the same story in yesterday’s hard-fought – but deserved – 2-0 win away at St Mirren.

It was hard to keep track of the number of times Min-su drifted in from the left-hand side to pick up possession with no opposition player within five yards. That’s not luck, it’s intelligence.

There is nobody playing in Scotland’s top flight more adept at taking the ball on the turn and driving into space either.

South Korean Kim Min-su contributes to all that is good about Rangers' attacking work

Min-su made life difficult for St Mirren during Rangers' 2-0 victory over the Paisley side

Dan Neil scores Rangers' second in a win that keeps them within four points of leaders Celtic

St Mirren couldn’t get near him for the majority of the first hour. They aren’t the first side to experience such difficulties, and they won’t be the last.

In full flight, he is a joy to watch operating in that pocket between the opposition midfield and defence.

It’s the bit after that where things start to become a little trickier for the talented 20-year-old.

He squandered a couple of opportunities to open his account here. The first came after playing a neat one-two with James Penrice late in the first half, with the ball sitting up perfectly for him ten yards out to smash home.

The choice to take one touch too many allowed Declan John to clear the danger.

So much of his game is based on instinct. Indeed, it’s a big part of what makes him such captivating viewing. But his decision-making in front of goal needs a lot of work.

Perhaps he’s guilty of overthinking things too much.

His manager certainly thinks so, admitting post-match that he felt Min-su was becoming ‘obsessed’ with registering his first goal for the club. In key moments, that shows.

A heavy touch early in the second period after being played in by Badredine Bouanani – unusually quiet here on the right – once again suggested he is feeling the pressure.

But let’s not forget, he’s essentially a kid trying to find his feet in a new country, and in a league which couldn’t be more different in terms of speed and style from what he was used to in Spain.

That he has actually managed to settle in so seamlessly should be applauded. It can’t have been an easy transition but he has quickly endeared himself to the supporters.

It’s why they are every bit as desperate as the player himself to get the monkey off his back.

They needn’t worry. If he keeps doing what he’s doing, the goals will come. Of that there is no doubt.

Some context has to be attached to his failure to notch an assist too. It’s a misleading stat, given that it depends entirely on someone else putting the ball away when it counts.

Min-su created multiple chances for his team-mates in Paisley, the best of which saw Kevin Kelsy put through on goal. It’s hardly his fault that the big man fluffed his lines. The Venezuelan has been in good form but had a stinker here.

At some point, everything will come together for Min-su. And it’s not as if he didn’t have an impact in both of Rangers’ goals against St Mirren.

It may have gone unnoticed amongst everything else, but he absolutely busted a gut to get himself into the box in the build-up to Dan Neil’s deflected strike which sealed the points on 61 minutes. That willingness to put the hard yards in off the ball is every bit as impressive as his ability on it.

And it was his pass to Penrice which led to the full-back being clipped by Samuel Ramos inside the box to give Rangers the opportunity to go ahead from the penalty spot early in the first half.

In truth, they may have been a little fortunate to do so. Put it this way, had referee Nick Walsh not given it, there’s not a chance in hell that VAR would have got involved.

Ryan Naderi stepped up to slot into the bottom corner to take his tally to nine for the season in all competitions.

It says a lot about where Naderi's head is that he had the confidence to do so, especially after blowing a great chance from six yards out only moments before. The German-born Czech international is a changed man, all right.

Speaking of confidence, there is no shortage of it at the other end of the park either. At times, the defensive pairing of Olwethu Makhanya and Emmanuel Fernandez look like they’re playing five-a-sides.

It’s usually the latter who throws in the odd lapse of concentration to add some peril to proceedings, but yesterday it was the normally dependable Makhanya’s turn to give his manager a few hairy moments. Thankfully for the South African, St Mirren couldn’t take advantage.

Craig McLeish’s men could have no complaints over the final result but could have made things interesting late on had either Eseosa Sule or Calvin Ramsay finished from close range.

It’s now just one win in nine for the Buddies, who – much like last season – just can’t seem to put the ball in the back of the net consistently. That problem plagued them so much that they ended up in the relegation play-off spot last year.

McLeish has done an excellent job since taking over from Stephen Robinson. A far better one than anyone could have possibly predicted. He has changed the style of this team completely in a very short space of time and so you have to trust he will be able to find a solution to their goalscoring issues too.

Rangers might be 13 points better off but they head into the international break also in search of that perfect balance.

When they’re on it, they’re very good. But they are still not commanding games from start to finish with any sort of regularity.

They won’t necessarily have to be pleasing on the eye to end up with their hands on the Premiership trophy come May. Celtic’s triumph last season proved that.

The Rangers supporters will gladly put up with imperfect displays for the next six months if that’s going to be the end result.

And if the likes of Min-su can hit the goal trail sometime soon, there’s a decent chance that’s exactly how things will play out.

#1278. Spalletti: ‘Juventus need to put faith in players, you say we must win Scudetto’

Luciano Spalletti explains his Juventus choices against Fiorentina with an all-new trident attack, and sarcastically hits back at critics. ‘You all say we need to win the Scudetto.’

It kicks off at the Stadio Artemio Franchi at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from today’s five Serie A games on the Liveblog.

The Bianconeri have a very poor recent record against their bitter rivals, not managing a victory since the 1-0 in April 2024, followed by two draws and as many defeats.

Weston McKennie and Zeki Celik are back in the squad, while Nick Woltemade came down with flu symptoms and is in the starting XI anyway as part of a new trident with Jeremie Boga and Randal Kolo Muani.

That means sending Kerim Alajbegovic to the bench this evening.

“We played two days ago, another three days before that, so we need to rest these players at some point,” Spalletti told DAZN Italia.

“Boga scored a great goal off the bench, he went t sit back down, so every now and then we have to put our faith in these players.”

Juventus had been plunged into crisis by the 3-0 home defeat to Lazio and 2-2 Rennes draw, but recovered with back-to-back wins over Napoli and AZ Alkmaar.

“It is a game where the volume will be turned up, in the crowd, on the field, it somehow becomes a bigger city when this game is one. So we must avoid getting manipulated or dragged into the frenetic nature of this fixture, we’ve got to keep our heads, and hopefully raise the quality level of our performance.

“You all say we need to win the Scudetto, so we’ve got to play with the quality that this squad does possess,” replied Spalletti with sarcasm to the Juventus critics.

“Being frenetic robs you of the right choice, it stops you seeing things clearly, so this can be a turning point for us.”

Juventus are still missing Kenan Yildiz, Andrea Cambiaso, Nico Gonzalez, Manuel Locatelli, Khephren Thuram and Kamil Grabara, with Jeff Ekhator only just returning from a long spell out.

“Ekhator is a physically strong centre-forward who can run into space, he has the strength to take a position against defenders and can hold up the ball. He is young, so he feels the pressure, as he probably did with these two injuries, he needs a little time, but we are happy to have him available as an alternative with different characteristics.”

#1277. Fruit, flies and getting frisky: how food odours trigger sexual arousal

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Thomas O. Auer is in the Department of Biology and at the Food Research and Innovation Center, University of Fribourg, 1700 Fribourg, Switzerland.

When the goddess Hera set out to seduce Zeus in Homer’s The Iliad, she did not start with her looks, but with perfume, preparing an ambrosial oil with a fragrance that filled “heaven and Earth”. The idea that scent kindles desire still captures our imaginations, but how odours act on the human brain to drive sexual attraction is unclear, and decades of searching for sex pheromones have produced no convincing candidates. That is not the case for insects, in which chemical sex signals are well understood. Writing in Nature, Brand et al.1 add another piece to the mosaic of sexual communication. By comparing fly species that are adapted to different host fruits, they show that food odours can be key for male sexual arousal. Flies combine this cue with information about their social environment to get into the mood for mating.

#1275. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

Emery had warned his players of complacency against the Norwegian champions, but Villa took command from the start and were ahead after 23 minutes.

Ross Barkley scored twice against Fenerbahce last week and was in the right place again to head Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner past Arild Ostbo.

Ross Barkley heads Aston Villa into the lead against Viking 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/gCFfr2iiVr

Hopes of another famous European night here never appeared likely, even though their 2,500 travelling supporters remained noisy all evening.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Champions League fixture as Aston Villa host Viking in the Midlands.

Villa made history in their previous home Champions League outing last week, thrashing Fenerbahce 6-0 to seal the club’s biggest-ever European win. However, after Michael Olise was sent off, Herman Haugen’s 90th-minute headed equaliser rescued a thrilling draw to give Viking their European point this season following a 3-1 loss to Stuttgart on MD1. #1273. Fabregas: ‘Inter deserved the victory, the strongest team in Europe in transition’

Cesc Fabregas admitted that Inter were the better side after Como fell to a 2-0 defeat in San Siro in Serie A on Sunday evening, explaining that the Nerazzurri have more experience in big matches and that they are ‘the strongest in Europe’ in transition.

Strikes from Pio Esposito and Marcus Thuram within the first 20 minutes gave Inter a two-goal lead against Fabregas’s side, which they were able to hold onto right the way through until the full-time whistle.

You can see how the action unfolded on the Football Italia Liveblog.

Fabregas did not need reminding that Inter were the better of the two sides on the pitch on Sunday. He was, in fact, complimentary of the way that Inter played and the experience they have available in their squad.

“We didn’t start the game well, we made a few mistakes and we weren’t confident,” Fabregas told DAZN while assessing his own side’s performance.

“We have to congratulate Inter, who played much better than us. We’re on a different journey than what we’re used to, playing every three games. We have to thank the boys for what they have given us so far.

“Inter deserved the victory, we have to shake their hands and move on. The demands are always rising and we have to continue like that. I’m not looking for any excuses, this is what football is like and a coach has to adapt. My responsibility is to look for solutions.

“We only had two central players, so I tried to help by bringing Smolcic in. The way we lost hurts, with those balls that we gave away too cheaply. That makes you lose confidence because Inter are very strong in transition, the strongest in Europe.”

Fabregas went on to explain that Inter “are one of the best teams around on counter attacks and from set-pieces. They made 13 fouls and did those well because they didn’t get any booking. In these games, just breaking up the rhythm can impact the game. These sorts of details show the experience they have and we’re lacking that.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1272. Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

The pace was perfect, allowing the Canadian not to break stride and stroke it past Raya. Kane did not fire the ball in, he did not make Davies work to reach it and he did not give Jurrien Timber any chance of cutting it out. It was perfect. Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

#1271. Celtic 1 Kilmarnock 0: Liam Scales scores only goal as Premiership leaders make hard work of it

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 15:06 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 15:06 EDT, 8 November 2026

For Martin O’Neill, the second international break of the season should be somewhat less fretful than the first.

Seven weeks ago, with a home defeat to Ferencvaros coming in between two no-shows against Rangers, the veteran wondered aloud if it might be time to ‘wrap it up’.

O’Neill later admitted that he regretted his choice of words. He won’t, though, lament the decision to go again as he rests up in the coming days.

While the intervening weeks have often been a bumpy ride, the past four days have been a lot more like it.

Thursday’s dramatic win over Besiktas has breathed new life into Celtic’s Europa League campaign.

While by no means spectacular, this narrow victory over Kilmarnock re-established their four-point lead at the top of the Premiership and will have further dampened the sense of hysteria which was threatening to engulf the entire club.

Celtic defender Liam Scales loops the ball over Kilmarnock's goalkeeper and into the net

Scales celebrates with Camilo Duran after netting the only goal of the game at Celtic Park

Celtic striker Kasper Hogh finds the net with a crisp right-foot shot, only to have it disallowed

Celtic certainly made hard work of this. Truth be told, they should have gone into the break on the back of a far more convincing victory.

While they were right to feel wronged that Kasper Hogh saw his goalless run stretch to 16 matches after having one harshly disallowed, O’Neill’s men did not help themselves either.

Coming after Liam Scales had given them a half-time advantage, Benjamin Nygren’s missed penalty allowed Kilmarnock to keep believing right to the end.

Nonetheless, it was hard to begrudge Celtic their victory over the piece. A few weeks back, this might have been a contest in which they’d have come a cropper. They look more assured defensively than earlier in the season.

You don’t need to stay up all night researching exactly why Kilmarnock are in such peril at this stage of the season.

Neil McCann’s side began the campaign losing goals and they’ve really never stopped. They cough up more chances than any side in the top division. When it comes to shooting themselves in the foot, they’re in a league of their own.

In 13 games to date, they’ve shipped 29 goals and have kept just two clean sheets in the process. St Mirren, the side with the second worst record in the Premiership, have lost 22.

As worrying as those statistics and the Premiership table undoubtedly are, though, this felt like a step in the right direction.

In being more resolute, McCann’s men stayed in the contest right until the final whistle. They fashioned a number of decent chances throughout. There was plenty of encouragement here, even though they went down again.

For the home supporters, the much-needed positivity which had emanated from Thursday’s European win was boosted by the return to the starting line-up of Jota for the first time since April 2025.

Notably, only three out of nine of Celtic’s summer signings made the squad, with Sam Johnstone the only one involved who arrived on deadline day.

O’Neill was indebted to the on-loan Wolves man inside the first minute. Ieuan Owen skipped away from Callum McGregor then Colby Donovan down the left and put in a dangerous cross. Twice Tom Lowery hit the target. Twice the Celtic keeper stood up tall.

Lowery immediately had his name taken by John Beaton for a clumsy foul on Nygren.

Despite their precarious position, to their credit, Kilmarnock didn’t come to Parkhead just to defend. Tyreece John-Jules, their main striker, had an abundance of support in the form of Owen, Greg Kiltie and Joe Hugill.

Between them, they fashioned enough half chances. They just didn’t have ice in the veins at the right moments.

Hogh was right to feel aggrieved at the decision which cost him that elusive goal. Truthfully, there was very little in Mika Baur’s challenge on Kiltie which was retrospectively penalised.

Duran gathered and fed Nygren. The Swede swivelled and rolled the ball into Hogh’s path. A crisp right-foot finish was not that of a player lacking in confidence.

The Dane’s lengthy celebrations included a look up to the heavens. By the time Beaton made his way to the monitor and chalked the goal off, Hogh could have been forgiven for feeling that someone up there had it in for him.

To Hogh’s credit, he didn’t let it affect him. Moments later, after being played in by Duran, he was only denied his revenge by the outstretched leg of Nico Mantl.

Hogh then played Duran in with a clever back-heel. The Colombian lashed his effort just wide.

Celtic’s pressure was mounting and they edged in front on 26 minutes with Duran, yet again excellent throughout, the architect.

His clipped cross from the right caught the Kilmarnock defence flat-footed. Scales extended his left foot and watched the ball rise to the point where it appeared to be going over.

With Mantl hoping that it would clear his bar, it looped into the net. There was no disputing this one.

Required to take more risks, Killie had to be careful when they turned the ball over. Hugill and Cathal McCarthy were both booked for crude fouls on Duran and Jota, respectively.

While Celtic began to control the affair, the visitors were not without their moments. Michael Schjonning-Larsen’s stinging strike from 25 yards forced Johnstone into another solid stop.

While Jota looked good in moments, it’s clearly going to take some time before he’s fully up to speed. The same might apply to Hyun-jun Yang, the man who replaced him at the interval, after being sidelined for six weeks with a hamstring injury.

Donovan came close to wrapping up the three points with an enterprising run and shot with his left foot which flew just wide.

Duran’s close control and speed across the ground bought him a yard for a shot. Having seen it late, Mantl dealt with it well.

Hogh actually performed well here. He was tidy with the ball and frequently brought team-mates into play. He just didn’t hit the target often enough. That again cost him when he spun neatly in the box and tried his luck midway through the second period.

You couldn’t fault him when he seized on Kieran Tierney’s cross, though. The saving block from Killie substitute MJ Kamson-Kamara was tremendous.

With the home supporters longing for a clinching second goal, Duran dumped a shot into the side netting before the industrious Baur was flagged offside after firing home.

The wait would go on. Initially adjudged to have struck Aaron Tshibola’s arm just outside the box, Yang’s strike would earn Celtic a spot-kick with 14 minutes remaining after a VAR review.

Nygren just never looked confident as he spotted the ball. Mantl dived to his right and made a comfortable save. Those hoping for a sharp exit sat back in their seats.

The sight of Baur hobbling badly after being caught by Tshibola didn’t make the viewing in the final moments any easier. All that truly counted for the home fans, though, was that Celtic got over the line.

#1270. Chivu: ‘Inter played as a team and were wonderful, last 9 games could’ve gone better’

Cristian Chivu was delighted with what he described as a ‘wonderful’ team display from Inter in their 2-0 victory over Como in Serie A on Sunday evening, and though he feels that the last nine matches could have ‘gone better’, he argues that they could have gone worse as well.

Strikes from Pio Esposito and Marcus Thuram within the first 20 minutes gave Inter a two-goal lead against Como, which they were able to hold onto right the way through until the full-time whistle.

You can see how the action unfolded on the Football Italia Liveblog.

The Como victory was Inter’s last game before the international break. They have played nine matches since the last round of international fixtures, which came to an end in October.

“I’d start by mentioning the fact that we’ve had nine games in 27 days, which has taken a lot of energy and brought lots of ups and downs,” said Chivu after full-time on Sunday.

“We always want to try and improve, but sometimes you have to swallow your pride and just work hard and prepare with the right mentality for the next games in front of you.

“Today, we raised the pace and intensity and our preparation served us well in terms of quality and pressure. We played as a team. We did well in the first half from all points of view, and then sometimes you need to know how to manage other moments of the game. I congratulate the boys, who were wonderful today.”

Chivu was asked whether the derby loss against Milan last weekend helped to spur on the Nerazzurri over the last week.

He said: “There’s always room for improvement. You can’t always have everything and be perfect every time. You have to accept that the season is long and there are lots and lots of games.”

Chivu is encouraged with the things that he is seeing from his players off the pitch as much as the things they do on it, praising the squad for holding each other to account.

“Things are in the right place. The injured players, the ones who are tired after getting back home at 4am after away games, all looking at each other when they win and when they don’t win. We lost the derby, but we had to move forwards. We have to pull in the same direction and carry on in what is a big and ambitious season.

“We need the right attitude. We reacted after losing in the derby and against Club Brugge, after which there was a lot of bitterness. After these last nine games, I can say that we definitely could have done better, but that we also could have done worse.”

Inter were able to stop Como from playing their own game in San Siro on Sunday, limiting their usually quality attacking play.

“It all starts with the forwards,” Chivu explained.

“They remained focused and took the ball away from them, arriving in the right place at the right time with their pressing. We knew that we needed to have compactness to cut off passing lanes. We knew that Como prefer to attack than defend. We were able to exploit what we had in our game plan.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.
