#1145. Spurs win three in row for first time in 616 days to pile pressure on Sage

For the first time in 616 days, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League matches in a row. Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

This victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. After Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute, Spurs simply had to make their numerical advantage count. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

Spurs take the lead through an Archie Gray header! ⚪ https://t.co/qSCECkOJur

Did this defeat mark the end for Pierre Sage, the Palace manager? The Frenchman was only appointed in June but it has been a grisly start to the campaign. Palace have the worst defence in the league, have lost six of nine games and have not produced any truly encouraging performances in the Premier League.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

“I am really aware of the situation,” Sage said. “I don’t like this situation. [But] you can trust in me, I will never give up. I want to be the first on the pitch on Monday. I have the rage to train more. It’s not me to decide this thing [his future]. If I have one hour, I will give my best for one hour. If I have 10 years, I will give my best for 10 years.”

The decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. It would be reasonable for Sage to claim this match was out of his hands from the moment Mateta lunged at Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, but such an argument might not carry much weight with Palace sitting 18th in the table.

The challenge was foolish in the extreme by Mateta, a player who was much more successful in exiting this game than he has been in his numerous attempts to leave Palace in recent transfer windows. At first glance it did not seem the worst tackle, but the replays were damning: Mateta led with his studs and made forceful contact with Van de Ven’s ankle.

It was an inexcusably brainless act, after just 13 minutes of play, and the same could be said of Palace’s defending from a right-wing corner a few minutes later. Mohammed Kudus swirled the delivery to the back post, where Gray was unmarked. Yes, Palace were defending with 10. But no, that does not justify the inability of Sage’s players to spot Gray. Even more embarrassingly, the Tottenham player was unmarked again from another corner shortly afterwards.

It was not the first time this season that Palace’s cause has been undermined by a red card. When they lost at home to Ipswich Town in September, Axel Disasi was sent off after 34 minutes. An absence of discipline? Perhaps. Sage might argue, though, that he is not responsible for his players demonstrating a lack of basic brainpower.

Jean-Philippe Mateta receives his first red card for Crystal Palace! 🟥 https://t.co/U9UYb29mbk

All of this was welcomed heartily by the Spurs fans, who celebrated Mateta’s dismissal as though it was a goal. Recent results have restored some of the enthusiasm in this corner of north London and the mood here was buoyant, even before Gray’s opener.

“Now we are playing as a team,” De Zerbi said. “Before the international break, we were playing as many good players but not as a team. We showed our maturity. We are improving.”

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League encounter between Tottenham and Crystal Palace.

Last weekend, Spurs enjoyed a historic result, beating Chelsea 2-0 at Stamford Bridge for only the second time in the league for 36 years thanks to Mike Penders’ own goal and Mathys Tel’s stunning solo strike. This result, coupled with the 3-1 victory over Coventry City in their previous home outing, means that Tottenham have won back-to-back league games and are beginning to gather some momentum under Roberto De Zerbi.

In his pre-match press conference, when asked if he’s felt a change in atmosphere after the triumph at Stamford Bridge, De Zerbi replied: “We have not achieved our goal. We want our fans to be happy, not now, at the end of the season. Now we have to push, we have to stay focused, we have to increase the spirit, the appetite to win games in a row. To do that, we have to show if we are good enough. If we are good enough on the pitch, for sure we are ready. In the head, in the mentality, we have to show, because the step of this club is to win games in a row and to be angry day by day, game by game, win by win. One time or two times are not enough.”

Palace have endured a tricky and inconsistent start to the season under their summer appointment Pierre Sage, accumulating just seven points from their opening seven league matches while shipping 17 goals. The 1-0 League Cup victory over Fulham in midweek has momentarily eased the pressure on the Frenchman, but given their newfound success in recent campaigns, fan expectations have risen, with recent performances prompting some cause for concern.

Tottenham remain without the suspended Rodrigo Bentancur, while Xavi Simons, Wilson Odobert, Lucas Bergvall, Savio, Tosin Adarabioyo and Mykhaylo Mudryk are out injured. The visitors are without the injured trio of Ismaila Sarr, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chadi Riad, but there’s hope that Quinten Timber and Jorgen Strand Larsen are fit to be involved this evening after they both missed the Fulham victory.

It's the end of an era: Cristiano Ronaldo, the Portuguese soccer star, announced his decision to retire from the Portuguese national team. Ronaldo, who will turn 42 next year, is considered one of the best players in the history of the sport, and announced his retirement from international soccer after 23 years representing Portugal, winning Euro 2016 and two editions of the UEFA Nations League. Cristiano followed the decision of his long-time rival Lionel Messi, who retired from the Argentine national team last month. Over his career with Portugal, he scored 146 goals in 234 games.

Portugal estará sempre em mim pic.twitter.com/dnFj51rxmh

Ronaldo's decision follows a rift with the current head coach Jorge Jesus. Last month, the striker left Portugal's training camp aboard his private jet following a disagreement with the coach, followed by an open letter and apologies to the fans and the team where he explained his decision, without mentioning the manager. The Portuguese federation later suspended the player for 30 days but he was eligible to be called for the upcoming games against Denmark and Wales.

Ronaldo posted a video message on his social media announcing his decision to retire from the national team: "To the Portuguese people, the day has come to hand back the number seven shirt of the national team that belongs to us all. I never felt it was exclusively mine. But for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and taking it with me to stadiums all over the world. Today the time has come to hand it over to the future. It was not an easy decision, because there are decisions that are not made solely with the head; they are also made with the heart."

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner played his sixth and last World Cup this summer in the United States, Canada and Mexico, when Portugal were eliminated by Spain in the round of 16 of the tournament.

"A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever is coming to an end. When I look back and think of everything I've experienced with the national team, I don't just see matches, goals, records or trophies. I see people. I see immigrants who, for 90 minutes, felt Portugal was a little bit closer. I see millions of Portuguese people whom I've never met in person, but who have been part of my life. Because, at the end of the day, football is so much more than just a game. Football is about the people. Throughout my entire career with the national team, I've strived to push my limits. I wanted to win, I wanted to be the best, I wanted to make history," he said.

"I've always been hard on myself. I've always wanted more; I've always believed we could go further. And I gave everything I had for this shirt. There were perfect afternoons and evenings; there were victories I'll never forget. There were defeats that I still find hard to recall today. I also failed, I also suffered, and there were moments when I wasn't able to give the Portuguese people what they so desperately wanted. But I never gave up. And above all, I never stopped feeling proud to represent Portugal. Over the years, I've learnt some very simple things. Goals come and go, trophies end up in museums, and records are eventually broken. But there is one thing that time can never erase: the place we hold in people's hearts. If I ever made you happy, if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget your worries, and feel nothing but pride in our country, then it was all worth it. Because that's what being Portuguese is all about. We suffer together, we rise together. No captain walks alone and you're all part of my story. Portugal will always need young people who dream, players who never give up, new generations who believe it's possible to reach places no one has reached before. Because a country that continues to create new heroes is a country that never stops believing in itself."

#1141. USMNT's Gold Cup path to look different as Concacaf unveils revamped group-stage format

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

For the United States men's national team to win their first Concacaf Gold Cup since 2021, they'll now need to contend with a new format in the 2027 edition. The tournament will run from June 17 through July 11, with major changes coming to the group stage. It will still include only 16 teams, but instead of those teams being split into four groups of four teams each, they'll now be split into only two eight-team groups. Fifteen of those teams will qualify via the Gold Cup preliminary round and join guest nation Saudi Arabia in the tournament.

That shift has the goal of making the group stage more exciting, as not only does it add an extra game due to each team playing four teams instead of three, but it also allows a chance for chaos, as four teams will go through to the knockouts from each group. While the new game is added, that won't change how the knockouts look, as those will proceed as normal.

"The Gold Cup is our region's premier men's national team competition, and we are really excited about what this new format will bring to the tournament's Group Stage," said Concacaf president and FIFA vice president Victor Montagliani. "Our fans want to see the best teams in our region compete against each other, and this format will create more opportunities for those matchups to happen earlier in the competition. At the same time, every match will matter, with teams facing a balanced mix of opponents and competing for a place in the knockout rounds. We believe this will make for a more competitive and exciting Gold Cup from the very first match through to the final."

How matchups are determined is where things get a little confusing, as they will organize the eight teams into ranking bands of two teams each, with a predetermined fixture matrix ensuring that each team plays a balanced schedule of opponents.

This is to prevent a situation where two strong Concacaf sides essentially ensure that others don't have a chance to advance, which could lead to more interesting fixtures in the knockout stages depending on how it goes.

🚨🏆 The rumors are confirmed! Gold Cup will have a whole new format in 2027. @FabrizioRomano breaks it down! pic.twitter.com/ydD1ZwbBvK

For the knockouts, nothing changes from how things used to look, as those four teams advancing from each group will then be placed into a single bracket, with the highest-finishing teams in each group facing off against the lower-finishing teams in the opposite group. There will then be no reseeding as the quarterfinals will determine the semifinal pairings in the road to the championship.

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

“This is a big win,” says Megan Peters, a cognitive scientist who moved in 2025 from the University of California, Irvine, to University College London, in part because of worries about US science. “It’s a demonstration that US [voters] are dissatisfied with what the current administration has been doing.” Scientific research, she adds, “is America’s superpower, and it’s been cut at the knees”.

Those hopeful for change include researchers affected by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) being shut down early in Trump’s presidency. “I’m cautiously optimistic,” says Quarraisha Abdool Karim, an epidemiologist at the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa, which is headquartered in Durban and had partnered with USAID on clinical trials. “What we’ve seen in the past 24 hours is that democracy and democratic principles, with individuals turning out to vote, can make a huge difference.” But, she adds, “we will not see overnight changes”.

As of 2.15 p.m. EST on 4 November, Democrats had secured at least 237 seats in the 435-seat US House of Representatives and 54 seats in the 100-member US Senate, giving them decisive majorities in both, with votes still being counted in some states. These majorities will give them the power to craft legislation that counteracts Trump’s science agenda, although there will still be obstacles. For instance, given that Democrats haven’t won two-thirds of the seats in both chambers of Congress, the president can veto those bills.

Trump initially told The New York Times that he would accept the mid-term election results and that he would “look forward” to working with Democrats. Later, however, he posted an image of a red hat with the word ‘VETO’ on it to Truth Social, his social-media platform.

Since Donald Trump became president for the second time in January 2025, his administration has pushed for unprecedented cuts to science funding, politicized decision-making at federal science agencies and interfered with policies at US universities that receive federal funding.

When Democrats take charge of both chambers of the US Congress on 3 January 2027, they will be able to control congressional committees, including science committees; set agendas for hearings that investigate government officials and their science policies; and use legally binding subpoenas to compel the Trump administration to provide documents and testify in front of Congress.

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

On social media, Democrats promised to make use of that authority. Robert Garcia, a representative from California who will soon chair the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, shared a two-word statement aimed at the Trump administration: “Lawyer up.” In particular, some scientists are calling for scrutiny of Russell Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, who has drafted a plan that gives political appointees, rather than scientist peer reviewers, control of decisions about research grants, and who has delayed the distribution of congressionally approved science funds.

Scientists and policy specialists said they were hoping to see more congressional oversight of the actions of Robert F. Kennedy Jr, the head of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), who has questioned vaccine safety, and whose tenure has coincided with the country’s worst measles resurgence in decades. “For sure, secretary Kennedy will be put on the hot seat” to explain his unscientific actions, says Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association in Washington DC. “What I’m hoping is that Congress will really push this administration to have a much more proactive response to the measles epidemic.”

Zoe Lofgren, a Democratic representative from California, said she would campaign to become the head of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, which oversees agencies such as NASA and the US National Science Foundation. “We will hold this administration accountable for the damage they have done to the American scientific enterprise,” she said in a statement.

Stand Up for Science, a science-advocacy group based in Atlanta, Georgia, that has organized protests against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science, says that it will release a plan on 5 November with strategies to push Congress for change.

Whether Congress will be able to increase funding for federal science, rather than just hold it relatively steady as they have for the past two years, is doubtful, however. Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, had protected science budgets, but she lost her re-election bid in these mid-terms. Large boosts to science spending could also just be difficult to pass, given that the budget must also be signed by Trump, who has tried to slash non-defence science spending.

#1136. Liverpool played like a team fighting for their manager, but Pierre Sage looks like a dead man walking, writes LEWIS STEELE - as Reds clinch morale-boosting win at sorry Crystal Palace

Published: 11:14 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 13:00 EDT, 8 November 2026

By this time of the season, spirited performances mean little if you don't have the results to go with it.

Pierre Sage, who was sacked at Lyon two years ago, knows as much as anyone that this is a results-based business.

And he simply has not had enough results. Despite having Liverpool on the ropes at times here, Crystal Palace failed to land a knockout blow and that could be that for their under-fire manager, who looked like a dead man walking when he trudged off the pitch at full-time with a face like thunder.

Former Lens over-achiever Sage now seems set for a stuffing six weeks before Christmas and though he may curse at the small margins that denied his team a chance of a heavyweight and potential job-saving scalp here, the boss knows two wins in 10 league games is not good enough.

Liverpool, meanwhile, had the width of the crossbar and a throwback performance from goalkeeper Alisson to thank. In contrast to Sage, Andoni Iraola's side showed grit and determination to win when far from their best.

Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak all scored as the Reds put a tough week behind them that saw them lose back-to-back games for the first time in the Iraola era, which prompted a chorus of the old terrace classic 'Poetry in Motion'.

Florian Wirtz scored a rare Liverpool as they won 3-1 at Crystal Palace in the Premier League

Wirtz scored Liverpool's second on 54 minutes as they ran out as 3-1 winners at Selhurst Park

Things are looking ominous for under-pressure Palace manager Pierre Sage after another loss

This performance was hardly William Wordsworth levels of poetry and Liverpool were far from on song during large swathes of this match but when it really mattered, the attackers demonstrated just why the club spent so much money on them.

CRYSTAL PALACE (3-4-2-1): Henderson 5; Lerma 6, Richards 6, Disasi 5; Mingueza 6 (Khalali 87), Wharton 5, Timber 6 (Timber 60, 6), Mitchell 6; Kamada 6, Pino 7 (McNeil 87); Larsen 5 (Nketiah 72, 7)

Subs not used: Benitez, Canvot, Chilwell, Doucoure, Hughes

LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1): Alisson 9; Araujo 7 (Gomez 90), Jacquet 6, Van Dijk 6, Kerkez 6; Szoboszlai 7 (Nyoni 69, 7), Mac Allister 8; Gakpo 6 (Ngumoha 76) Wirtz 8, Barcola 7 (Munoz 69, 7); Isak 7 (Koumas 90)

Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Endo, McConnell, Tsimikas

Booked: Araujo, Barcola, Munoz, Mac Allister

Scorers: Mac Allister 40, Wirtz 54, Isak 89

Mac Allister resumed his bemusing role of the team's best aerial threat despite being their smallest player, Wirtz got a goal and assist, while Isak made it eight for the season to continue his prolific streak.

Bradley Barcola, meanwhile, proved what an asset he is despite a wasteful first half.

Those attackers were worthy of praise but no one deserved plaudits more so than goalkeeper, Alisson, who was player of the match in an illustration of Palace's first-half supremacy.

'I'm very pleased with Alisson's performance,' said Iraola. 'He has commanded the box very well and in games here a lot of things are normally happening in the boxes. He has shown the level he has for us. Overall we are getting good results away from home at difficult stadiums.'

The Brazilian is in the last year of his contract but put in his best performance for 18 months, dating back to a 1-0 win at Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League knockouts. He will not go on international duty and instead rest up after an injury-hit few years.

He denied Adam Wharton with a glancing header, thwarted Daichi Kamada with a fierce shot and then tipped round Quenten Timber's effort from distance. Palace also rattled the bar through Yeremy Pino in a first half that really should have ended up differently.

Jorgen Strand Larsen also had the ball in the net but was offside.

As it was, though, Liverpool were the team to take their chance when it came after a period of dilly-dallying and playing the wrong ball, guilty again of indecisiveness similar to the flaws shown against Arsenal last weekend and in the 3-2 defeat at Fenerbahce in midweek.

Liverpool led on 40 minutes when Alexis Mac Allister (centre left) scored from close range

The Argentine celebrates after breaking the deadlock for the Reds in the Premier League clash

Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage is facing the sack after his side dropped to the bottom of the Premier League.

Palace have won just two of their ten league matches this season, with Sunday's 3-1 defeat to Liverpool leaving them at the foot of the league for the first time in nearly nine years.

Sage is expected to lose his job during the international break, with Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank leading the race to replace the French coach.

However, Sage believes his side have been unlucky with results this season and has requested the hierarchy remain patient.

The 47-year-old, who left RC Lens for Palace in the summer to succeed Oliver Glasner, also admitted the Palace squad needs strengthening - perhaps to absolve himself of some blame.

'You can create the links between these two things,' Sage replied when asked whether being bottom of the league heading into the international break could see him sacked.

'But a lot of times I've said we deserved better and it was the case again on Sunday.

'My job is not the most important thing, as I always said from the beginning. The most important thing is to find an efficient solution for the team and for the club.

'I know how important it is for the club to stay in the Premier League. The club just have to believe in that, and if it's not the case, they will take a decision.

'I always have confidence in myself because it's a big, big mistake to not be 100% involved in what I have to do.

'We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions and more efficiency and I think it will be okay.'

Mac Allister was the scorer as he continued a fine resurgence this season, with Dominik Szoboszlai the supplier after a week where he too had been criticised. The Hungarian whipped a cross towards Mac Allister, which was glanced past Henderson for 1-0.

The former Brighton player ran straight towards the Palace fans behind the goal and taunted the supporters that were once his rivals on the south coast.

Liverpool weathered another storm at the start of the second half and soon found themselves two up. Barcola, who had left lots to be desired in the first half, swapped wings at the break and made his first attack count.

The Frenchman put the after-burners on and motored down the pitch before feeding Wirtz, who composed himself and passed into the net for 2-0. Iraola praised the run of Isak which took him away from the ball but dragged defenders with him to create space for his colleague.

Isak squandered a one-versus-one chance not long after but was not going to miss another one minutes later, when a blisteringly quick counter-attack was started by Trey Nyoni and ended with Wirtz feeding Isak, who skipped past Chris Richards and finished calmly.

The three goals will delight the hierarchy, with all three of the £100m boys – Isak, Barcola and Wirtz – registering at least one goal or assist apiece, one each in Wirtz's case.

Alexander Isak scored the visitors' third in the 89th-minute with this right-footed finish

Eddie Nketiah pulled one back for Palace from the penalty in second-half stoppage time

This victory would not have been possible, though, without Alisson, now 34 and in the final year of his deal. For all the attacking talent at Iraola's disposal, the Basque will be delighted at his team's defensive determination when under the kosh here as Palace had 10 first-half shots.

Iraola knows his team has flaws and they remain a work-in-progress. But despite a few challenging afternoons, they appear to be heading in the right direction.

The same cannot be said for Sage, whose side pulled one back in stoppage time through an Eddie Nketiah penalty after Milos Kerkez committed a careless foul.

Palace were unlucky in this game but the cold, hard truth is that the recent FA Cup and Europa Conference League triumphs feel a world away now as they enter the international break rock bottom of the Premier League.

West Ham also won a European trophy in the last five years and look where they ended up — that should set alarm bells ringing that no success lasts for ever and Palace are not too big for relegation.

Nketiah's goal felt like it was too little, too late and the sage advice for Palace supremo Steve Parish might be a reluctant change in the dugout.

Two matchdays remain in the Apertura portion of the Liga MX season, and there's everything to play for, from the title down to the final playoff spots. CBS Sports Golazo Network will be the place to see plenty of the key action. Club America lead Chivas Guadalajara and Cruz Azul only on goal difference, while Atlas are also a surprise contender for the title, trailing by only two points. Club America may have the best attack in the league, with Henry Martin leading the line and getting back to his best, but a potentially tricky matchup with Pumas could cost them points.

Club America have lost only twice this season, but they have scuffled a bit and are winless in their last three, including a loss to Pachuca, who are led by the league's top scorer in the ageless Salomon Rondon. At the opposite end of the spectrum, the final four playoff spots are essentially up for grabs, as anyone currently fifth to 11th could be passed, and only four teams have been mathematically eliminated from playoff contention.

Technically, Puebla are done if anyone on 22 points secures a point, but even the fact that they have a chance in 14th place shows how competitive this season has been. But it's also one that could bring quite a shock if the table ends as it is currently, with Monterrey on the outside looking in at the playoffs.

Date: Saturday, Nov. 7 | Time: 8 p.m. ETLocation: Estadio Nemesio Diez -- Toluca de Lerdo, MexicoLive stream: CBS Sports Golazo NetworkOdds: Toluca -170; Draw +340; Monterrey +360

Traveling away to face Toluca, Rayados need all the points that they can get and then some. They haven't missed the playoffs since 2016, and despite being the third-highest-spending team, behind Atlas and Club America, there hasn't been much to show for it as Matias Almeyda's chaotic management follows the squad through the season. They have talent in the squad, but it's not all coming together all at once. This team is just as likely to win 4-2 as it is to lose by the same score, and that comes down to management, not talent.

On talent, there's no reason for Monterrey to miss the playoffs, and having three of the top 15 scorers on their team shows that this is an attack to be feared. It's anyone's guess if they'll actually get things together in time, but if it doesn't happen Saturday night, only 90 minutes will remain before missing the playoffs becomes reality for the club.

#1129. Suzuki howler costs Aston Villa crucial points

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

“I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager said. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

“I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

“We have to change our mind quickly for Tuesday against Barcelona. We want to test ourselves at this level.”

Villa go to the Nou Camp with a 100 per cent Champions League record to their name this season. But they will need to improve on Saturday evening’s performance to get a result in Spain.

As well as Suzuki’s error, a 14th-minute penalty miss from John McGinn also proved costly.

It was awarded after Leon Goretzka, making his full league debut for Villa, saw his header hit Sander Berge’s raised hand. Nobody appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor by VAR to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

McGinn’s attempt, however, hit the crossbar and the chance to take an early lead went begging. The Villa captain seemed a strange choice to take the spot-kick as he has only ever scored one career penalty, but Emery defended the choice, saying: “We analysed the penalty takers in the squad and it was McGinn here.”

Nicolas Jackson was on hand to ease Villa’s nerves before the break, though. the Villa manager had said before the game that the striker’s goalscoring capability meant he was capable of matching the likes of Harry Kane. Collecting Johan Manzambi’s superbly weighted pass, Jackson forced his way past two defenders before sliding in the goal that put Villa ahead.

Emery’s touchline celebrations said it all as the Senegal forward continues to flourish under the man who knew how to get the best out of him at Villarreal.

Robinson put in another cross and Suzuki got a touch that was enough to make Garcia put his shot wide. Villa were living dangerously and the Japanese goalkeeper made another outstanding stop to keep out Iwobi’s header. But then it all went wrong for Suzuki when he fumbled Iwobi’s corner.

That allowed Fulham’s recent revival under manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, to continue – they now have seven points from their past three games.

“We spoke at half-time about what we had to do,” Arbeloa said. “If you want to win a game you have to fight and I think we have to believe in our way, we’ve shown we can beat anyone in the way that we play but we have to be aggressive.

Zion Suzuki had big gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”

Emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

But the Spaniard said: “For different reasons, not only rest.”

Whatever he meant is unclear, but both start for Villa tonight.

Fulham have won their last two league games – against Hull and Coventry.

Manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, has made one change with Sander Berge replacing Hugo Larsson in midfield.

Villa are aiming to win three successive league games for the first time in this calendar year. The omens are good as they’ve beaten Fulham in their last seven league meetings at Villa Park.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

#1128. Chasing dynasty: How Gotham FC's NWSL Shield win completes transformation ahead of playoffs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

En route to their second NWSL championship in two years, relatively new Gotham FC recruit Jaedyn Shaw was uninterested in the narratives that underestimated her team. The surprise win at the NWSL Shield-winning Kansas City Current in the playoff quarterfinals was not a surprise to her, and she made it clear with three quick words: "Underdog, my ass."

Shaw had a point on that cold day in the Midwest, and almost exactly a year later, it still stands. Gotham are the NWSL's new dynasty, and their Shield win marked their fifth major title in three years, with a sixth in their sights as the playoffs begin this weekend. The transformation was rapid for a team that has historically been a bottom-dweller, so much so that their 2023 championship triumph was a genuine surprise. They quickly built a title-winning team and reaped the rewards just as swiftly, but even as the muscle memory of title charges returns, Gotham will go about their next NWSL playoff journey differently. The target is officially on their backs, the onus officially on them to live up to the billing.

Gotham have played the vast majority of their playoff games as the lowest-seeded team in the postseason, winning the championship twice in those circumstances. Sunday's quarterfinal against the Seattle Reign, though, will be the first game they play as the unquestionable favorites to win the whole thing. How Gotham will play with the weight of expectations is entirely unclear, since they have never done it before, but it is a good problem of their own creation, one they have chased since the 2023 triumph.

Date: Sunday, Nov. 8 | Time: 12:30 p.m. ETLocation: Sports Illustrated Stadium -- Harrison, N.J.TV: ABC | Live stream: ESPN AppOdds: Gotham FC -150; Draw +265; Seattle Reign +340

Their blitz in the free-agent market in the winter of 2024 laid the foundation for their dynastic run, but the most fascinating feature of Gotham's years-long run of success is the evolution they have undergone since. U.S. women's national team defender Tierna Davidson has become the team's captain, her progressive passing ability making her a key fixture in head coach Juan Carlos Amoros' system. Her club and country teammate Rose Lavelle has become a standout, but the star of the show has been Shaw, who has barely missed a beat since her arrival in September 2025.

Shaw has 14 goals and seven assists in 35 NWSL games with Gotham, her wide-ranging skill set fully on display in Amoros' team. She has been a little bit of everything for the team's attack, which is arguably too reliant on her talents, but it is almost hard to fault Amoros for the approach. The system has allowed Shaw to flourish, in particular bringing out a clear goal-scoring quality that is key to a Gotham team that values defensive work rate first.

"First, I think the commitment they have to defend and the commitment they have to work hard for the team despite being some of the best players technically in the planet," Amoros said about both Shaw and Lavelle after a win over the Chicago Stars in September. "I think that helps the connection, not only between them two. There is a mutual respect there because of that but then also from the whole team. When you have to play and those are the players that produce the chances for us in the final third but then the people that [are] behind them are always supportive of them because of the work they put in and then we try to work a lot with them to how we can find them and how they can connect more with each other and the same with Sam [Kerr]."

He has found a unique way to make Shaw and Lavelle work together, despite the fact that they appear to have overlapping skill sets when it comes time for USWNT head coach Emma Hayes to slot them into her lineup. The pair often play just behind Kerr, an out-and-out striker, and assume the role of strikers themselves while balancing their creative tendencies. They have filled in some gaps along the way -- Kerr, for example, ranks third in the league with 9.67 expected goals since returning to the NWSL on July 16 but has scored just four times. Kerr does, though, have four assists in 17 games, one fewer than Shaw and one more than Lavelle over that span.

The connection between Lavelle and Shaw has offered Gotham a level of dynamism that has been missing in their attack at times over the years, even as they racked up title after title. It helps that the two have enjoyed working alongside each other, the 21-year-old Shaw in particular taking inspiration from Lavelle, a decade her senior.

"I think her movement is some of the best in the world, honestly," Shaw said after that September win over the Stars. "She's able to make stretch runs, drag players. She attracts so many players, opening up space for other players to get on the ball and then getting on the second one, I think, is one of her strengths and is something I'm trying to replicate off of her. I think she's just incredibly smart in soccer knowledge."

For each of them, a return to fitness after small injuries in the final weeks of the regular season comes not a moment too soon. Kerr's inconsistency is not the only attacking issue they will need to overcome -- Jordyn Dudley will miss the postseason with a foot fracture she sustained last month, her impressive rookie season coming to a close with four goals and three assists. Lavelle and Shaw will be particularly useful against the Reign, whose defensive qualities continue to be a strength.

Shaw has become the focal point of Gotham's reinvention in recent years, but Amoros' side has added experienced options in a wide variety of positions since the 2023 championship. The vast majority of Gotham's likely starters on Sunday will have joined the club after the 2023 playoff run, a steady stream of important players signing themselves up since. Ann-Katrin Berger, the 2024 goalkeeper of the year, made the move not long after Davidson and Lavelle did, and European champion Jess Carter followed right after. Midfielder Jaelin Howell, who has been in and around the USWNT, was recruited in time for the 2025 season, and Shaw joined months later. Left back Guro Reiten has two goals and six assists since making her club debut in April, while Kerr made the move at roughly the same time as midfielder Denise O'Sullivan, a two-time NWSL champion with the North Carolina Courage.

Gotham's reinvention is constant, the core evolving each and every season. It is a unique route to the top, but in another season of change, they found the consistency they have been chasing since the 2023 championship. The underdog label has well and truly been shed, the team chasing another tag entirely -- a third championship would put them level with the Portland Thorns as the most successful team in the league's history.

#1126. This is how Enzo Maresca's tactics have left Elliot Anderson exposed with too much to do, writes JACK GAUGHAN... and why £125m Enzo Fernandez must step up and offer much more to solve midfield riddle

Published: 07:00 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 13:08 EDT, 8 November 2026

Manchester City spent £320million on overhauling their midfield over the summer. In doing so, they twice broke their own transfer record. This marked the most aggressive focus on a specific need since the lavish outlay on full backs nine years ago.

All signed weeks before the independent commission’s guilty verdicts were announced, Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi heralded a new era in the City engine room. More energy, vibrancy, dynamism.

Two of them were ready-made replacements for Rodri and Bernardo Silva, with Bouaddi only 18 at the time and purchased as a potential superstar after shooting to global prominence at the World Cup.

But as Enzo Maresca heads into the second international break of the season on the back of three consecutive Premier League defeats, his midfield is the primary area of concern. And has been for a while.

A big fortnight lies in store for City’s manager, whose midfield has been wide open all year. Fine when outscoring opponents – see the 5-3 victory over Sunderland – and it makes for great entertainment yet an obvious gaping chasm when the goals dry up slightly.

The balance has not felt right and Maresca, who has gently batted away persistent questions about the midfield for weeks, must know this.

Elliot Anderson is being asked to do too much and it cost City in the 3-1 defeat at Forest

While studying tapes of all three defeats over the coming days, before City come back after the internationals to host Fulham and then go to Arsenal, he needs to determine a plan moving forward and that will include some tough decisions on individuals and shapes.

Nottingham Forest could have driven a bus through the middle of the park on Saturday night, two goals from counter-attacking situations engineered between the width of the centre circle. Twice the ostensible holding midfielder Anderson tried to nick possession, beaten to it, and City were turned around.

Noises coming from the dressing room suggest that Anderson is effectively being asked to operate as both a No6 and No8 when picked as the deepest of the three, to go and join play high up the pitch. That is Maresca leaning into the England international’s Action Man, everything to everyone style. That also relies on somebody covering for him.

That somebody does not exist in this current setup, Fernandez always too high and wide elsewhere.

So when they lose duels as happened at the City Ground, something the manager openly bemoaned, City are not stable enough to recover.

Liam Delap's fierce finish put Forest 2-0 ahead - and City were left playing catch-up

Club analysts have sat down with Anderson to go over video clips on how best to follow these instructions to the benefit of the team. Watching him, it’s hard not to conclude that this is a quality midfielder being asked to do too much as a single deep midfielder.

England are sweating on the fitness of Marc Guehi as the Manchester City defender battles a hip injury.

Guehi came off at half time of Saturday's 3-1 defeat by Nottingham Forest, with Thomas Tuchel's squad set to link up in London on Monday morning.

With John Stones already out of Nations League ties with Croatia and Spain, Tuchel would be severely light on experience at centre half should Guehi not prove his fitness.

It will produce moments of sheer class – that lung-busting run up the right in Leipzig on Wednesday that bore hallmarks of Kevin De Bruyne, a perfect cross for Erling Haaland’s winner – while also leaving the defence exposed.

An exposed defence lends itself to a heightened chance of individual errors, plenty of those around at the moment, and it was noticeable at Forest that the opening goal came from uncertainty in possession. Josko Gvardiol made the error, eased off the ball by eventual goalscorer Jair Cunha, but the plan cannot be to have the left back with his back to goal and no viable passing options.

When Marc Guehi’s ball went into Gvardiol, Anderson was higher and wider on the right – deep in conversation with Abdukodir Khusanov about how they’d failed to move possession well enough earlier in the sequence – and Rayan Cherki was belatedly trotting back to offer himself.

Fernandez never once enters the frame, even when Cunha is in the box and subsequently wheeling away in celebration. Maresca rejected the suggestion that there is an issue with the team’s build-up on Saturday night.

As Man City look to build from the back in the third minute, Anderson (No 5) is busy delivering instructions to Khusanov (out of shot)...

... it means that when Guehi plays the ball to Gvardiol, he has his back to goal and nobody in midfield to pass to - and is already under pressure

... and with no support, three Forest players swarm and Jair Cunha dispossesses him, leading to him scoring the opening goal

What is clear though is that there is not yet that balance, that this is not yet a unit. Maresca moved to include Bouaddi with Anderson and Fernandez against Brighton – a one-goal defeat – but that acted as detrimental to creativity. If nothing else, Brighton proved that City require either Cherki or Phil Foden on the pitch at all times.

Over the past two games, Fernandez has lurked more menacingly at the back post, offering an additional goal threat rather than just relying on Haaland. That ghosting late run saw him score in Leipzig but for a joint-British record £125million needs to offer so much more. There will be growing calls for Bouaddi’s inclusion as a genuine deep-lying midfielder but it’s unlikely that the teenager can manage the league’s physicality as a single pivot.

The Moroccan has more chance of stamping his authority when alongside somebody else, dovetailing with an Anderson as a two. That leaves Fernandez, whose barnstorming league debut at Old Trafford feels like a long time ago now.

To persist with him, he either dislodges Cherki as the No10 on the promise of far more goals or Maresca drops him back into a more conventional role that allows Anderson to flourish properly.

Something has to give because the unevenness of City’s three is giving the rest of the team uncomfortable jitters.

#1124. Kai Havertz leads the Premier League in offsides as Arsenal pile up infractions in 1-0 win over Hull City

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LONDON -- Though there was some to-ing and fro-ing as to the order in which the offenses should be considered, it seemed fitting that what would have been Arsenal's best scoring chance of the first half of their 1-0 win over Hull City was wiped out for an offside. Here is a team whose attack has been drifting so out of sync that promising situations fall apart without the opponent needing to get involved.

Sometimes the opponent is even willing to offer them a helping hand. Only the members of the International Football Association Board might be able to say for sure whether Arsenal should have had a penalty when Kai Havertz's shirt was pulled by Hull City's Nobel Mendy as Bruno Guimaraes took a long-range shot. The striker was impeded, but he had been standing in an offside area. Was he attempting to play the ball when Mendy grabbed hold of his jersey? If not, then the foul should have taken precedence and Arsenal should have had a penalty. Instead, they had to wait until the 72nd minute for their win, Martin Odegaard bundling in the rebound off Noni Madueke's shot.

At least that meant Mikel Arteta could jokingly say he had not seen the spot kick that might have been. There may be a question about that particular penalty and offside, but the big-picture statistics are mind-boggling, such that there surely has to be some air in these numbers.

In the last seven Premier League seasons, no team has averaged more than three offsides per game. Only Burnley in 2021-22 and Liverpool two years later have averaged more than 2.5, in the process reaching over 100 for the season. In their 10th game of the season, Arsenal committed offside offenses Nos. 32, 33, 34 and 35. At the final whistle, that was 11 more than any other team in the league, and there is a very real prospect that lead does not get eaten into. Field a team of Pippo Inzaghis and you'd do well to put up these numbers.

There has to be something to this, right?

What makes this all the more curious is that Arsenal have not been a team that particularly struggled to stay onside before this season. In the previous six campaigns, they were caught about as often as the average Premier League team when you adjust for possession. When these relatively low-volume statistics warp like this, at least part of the answer is going to be variance. A bit more of it might be that Arsenal have a 10-game sample size that includes Aston Villa. Still, that sample is over a quarter of the season. Arsenal have had a string of games where they have been caught offside with frequency.

This looks like a problem. Even Arteta acknowledged that. "There are many areas that we need to improve. That's one, that's related sometimes to the timing or the situation, or really the position [of the opponent], where he's lined up and what space he's given you.

"Certainly it's far too many. It's true that the Villa game obviously he's putting those stats in a different perspective. I think the sample is quite short to analyse it, but you have a point there."

As for the Villa game, Mikel, yes, that's eight of your 35. Leeds is seven, though. Coventry five, Hull four. These are all well above the Premier League average. The chief culprit for this spate of infractions is certainly Havertz. His 15 offsides are not just seven more than any other player in the top flight; they are more than any Arsenal player committed in the entirety of last season's title campaign.

Again, this feels a little unprecedented. In the six seasons prior to this one, Havertz ranked 48th among forwards in the division for how frequently they were caught offside. The worst offenders, your Ashley Barneses, Darwin Nunezes and Cristiano Ronaldos, might get flagged once every 70 or 80 minutes. Havertz hovered around the 140 mark. This season it's not far off once per half.

Has he lost some burst? Gradient Sports' physical data would suggest he is moving about as swiftly this season as any other. A broader view is that this attack might have greater joy punishing high lines with more pacey options in it. For a player who makes so many runs off the ball, Madueke is caught offside relatively infrequently (though his was one of the four today). That is probably because he can give his man a yard in a way that Havertz or even Bukayo Saka, third in the league with seven offsides, can't quite.

Have defenses sussed Havertz's movement out? That doesn't seem entirely clear, not least given that Hull misjudged their line more than once, allowing Havertz in a one-on-one position where he should have done much better than cut the ball onto Mendy's trailing leg.

Arteta's explanation is simple. "It's all about timing," he said. "So there is a signal on the ball, and you need to time it around that. If that's a second too late or half a second too late, that's all."

Certainly Arsenal could release the ball a bit quicker. If there is a flaw in the game of Odegaard, whose nine passes to an offside teammate also lead the league, it is that he tends to want that one extra touch. That much was apparent in the win at Aston Villa, when the captain had the ideal chance to slip Havertz through in position to bend one in the far post. He took three touches when two would have sufficed, and it was all a moment too late.

Bruno Guimaraes (four such passes) is in a similar vein. And perhaps Arsenal as a club are a bit too much of that ilk. Does the specter of Alex Hleb and Samir Nasri still haunt this team? Arteta might have said as much, that the thing about Arsenal is they always try to walk it in.

"We need to find ways to be more efficient, sometimes even more pragmatic," he said. "Sometimes my feeling is that we are trying to score a perfect goal against these low blocks. We need to be much more chaotic than that."

You can see that in some of those offsides above, especially the smattering around the right flank that Arsenal like to make their creative hub. It's the attempted reverse balls, the quick one-twos and slide-rule passes to a teammate on the overlap. Offside No. 36 might well have been another of those, an overlapping run from Jurrien Timber where Madueke released the pass a beat too late and the Dutchman stopped rather than cede Hull a free kick.

Instead, Madueke proved the value of an alternative approach right throughout this match. Driving at his fullback time and time again, he manufactured positions where things might happen without having to worry about a give-and-go or timing his run correctly. In an age where so many opponents, including Hull, are more intent on gumming up their opposition than gritting and grinding, a bit of unpredictability from one of Arsenal's own players goes a long way. As for the offsides, of course that feels like a problem, a lot of possessions wasted by Arsenal players' own inability to get on the right beat. It has been. It does not mean it is going to be. Injuries mean that Havertz and Odegaard have rarely shared the pitch over the last few seasons. Get them and Saka together for weeks on end and the old rhythm will come back to them, and this should be nothing more than a weird, if intriguing, blip.

#1121. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

I have learnt that you can only take the table seriously in February and March and all you can do until then is win as many as you can.”

Barcola’s last-gasp cross is blocked and that is that.

Arsenal have won at Anfield for the first time since 2012.

Hincapié fouls Ngumoha in the Liverpool box. Alisson launches it and Gabriel throws himself on to the floor after a touch from Isak and Arsenal have a free-kick.

Isak is caught in the offside trap when chasing Barcola’s hook over the top that could have put him through one-on-one.

Barcola cannot impart any power on a shot from eight yards after he pounced following some pinball passes and ricochets. Raya easily stops it. A shot on target.

Munoz, sandwiched between Hincapie and Calafiori, manages to get his head on Koumas’s flick on at the back post bit cannot get any power on it.

Ngumoha’s shot is deflected behind for a corner.

Van Dijk is playing as a centre-forward now but Gyojkeres’ lack of pace ruins Arsenal’s chances of exploiting his absence at the back from a counter-attack when he can’t get to Lewis-Skelly’s upfield pass.

Calafiori blocks Ngumoha’s left-foot shot out for a throw-in.

Calafiori shins a pass into touch when under pressure from Ngumoha. Still no Liverpool shot on target.

Hincapié goes to left-back with Calafiori in front of him.

Koumas → AraujoMuñoz  → WirtzTsimikas → Kerkez

Mac Allister goes down clutching his head after winding up Arsenal with a slap on Odegaard. Madueke had narrowed the gap and touched Mac Allister’s forehead with his own but sanity prevails and Madueke is not sanctioned. Mac Allister and Timber are booked.

Liverpool keep huffing and puffing around the Arsenal box but the champions seem more and more convinced that their house is made of bricks.

You will go a long way this season before you see a better save than the one Alisson Becker has just produced to keep Liverpool in the contest. Van Dijk leathers a shot from 25 yards that loops up over to the right. Ngumoha chases it and keeps it in, working it back to MacAllister whose cross is plucked out of the air by Raya.

Liverpool defend the corner though at the price of going down to 10 because Kerkez went down after a collision of heads.

Arsenal waste a few seconds after Van Dijk was penalised for a foul on Bruno. They decide to take him off but even when the substitution is completed, they still dawdle over the restart.

Mac Allister, in shooting territory 25 yards out, tries to fizz a pass to Wirtz in the box instead and Arsenal scramble it away.

Both players receive rousing receptions on departure and entry.

Liverpool take the free-kick quickly and Kerkez releases Isak down the left to lash a left-foot shot over the angle of left post and crossbar.

Madueke is booked for legging up Barcola who threatened to race away on a counter after Van Dijk had blocked Bruno’s shot.

Arsenal hold their nerve and their lines when Wirtz, Nyoni and Gakpo try to thread passes in to feet in the penalty area, managing to make the blocks as Liverpool keep probing.

Arsenal set up solidly in defensive lines to stop Liverpool raising the tempo on which they thrived in the first half.

Araujo wends his way around Calafiori after good work from Isak and crosses towards the penalty spot. Gabriel hooks the ball away with Wirtz and Isak on their heels around the 18-yard line.

Victor Muñoz has gone through a rigorous half-time warm up, which indicates he won’t be far away from getting minutes. Liverpool re-start “kicking into the Kop” in the words of Ian Wright. A ling chip down the right gives Gakpo something to chase but he can’t get round Calafiori who shepherds it out for a goal-kick.

With two minutes of stoppage time signalled Arsenal are on a rare attack but Tozolis again doesn’t release the ball when he should and slows it down.

Liverpool seem intent on trying to score a perfect goal. The irony is that it’s old fashioned pace and being direct that is starting to unsettle Arsenal. Bradley Barcola, therefore, needs to step up. Mac Allister misses a sitter. He eluded his midfield marker and met Kerkez’s perfect cross between the penalty spot and six-yard line but steered it over. Now it’s Calafiori’s turn to upbraid the players ahead of him.

Timber is penalised for a decent-looking tackle on Isak just outside the box on the Liverpool left. That comes a moment after the referee gave Liverpool a corner despite Mac Allister’s cross not touching an Arsenal player. They are going spare and one can sympathise with them.

Kerkez cushions a pass on his thigh when he ghosts into the centre-forward position and then tamely lobs a volley wide from 18 yards. Liverpool are swarming the Arsenal penalty area.

Liverpool are laying siege at the moment, snapping into tackles, putting in crosses, taking one too many touches to surprise Arsenal. Now Gakpo goes down in the box when confronted by Tzolis who does make contact but not enough for Madley or the VAR after a look.

Liverpool corner from the right. Van Dijk wins the header and Isak, creeping round Konsa, is there to tap it in, but Raya is alert and pushes it behind before Isak can pounce.

Tzoli’s cross from the left is met at the back post by Timber who tries to knock it back across the six-yard box to Havertz but Timber gets in the way.

Mac Allister’s crossfield pearler picks out Kerkez but he hits the first defender with his cross and Arsenal counter at pace and Madueke faces Kerkez up but dawdles instead of trying to dribble past him. Arsenal have come with one intention in mind, seemingly, and that is to spoil the game. Already in the opening 14 minutes we have seen Gabriel go down as if he had been cracked on the chin by Tyson Fury and now Kai Havertz has reacted bizarrely to a straightforward coming together with Virgil van Dijk. They are better than that, as they have just shown with Havertz’s opening goal, and Liverpool will have to be cute if they are to find a way back into the contest.

Odegaard pushes up behind Tzolis and frees the winger for a run into the box. Araujo stalsk him stride for stride and uses his strength to lever him off the ball which rolls out for a goal-kick.

Arsenal are dominating possession but when they go back to Raya he makes a rare error with his feet and launches a 50-yard pass over Madueke’s head into touch.

Nyoni gets away without a card after another foul, this one on Havertz when Nyoni’s touch let him down and he booted the Arsenal forward. Mikel Arteta is rightly peeved that the referee has let him off again. Youth buys you leeway with Andy Madley.

Liverpool counter at pace down the middle but Raya is very sharply off his line to deal with the long pass. That’s the source of all the jargon about ‘verticality’ both managers inflicted on us in the build-up.

Arsenal corner after Tzolis was given space to run into down the left but hit Jacquet with his square pass when he made the 18-yard line. Arsenal take it short and seem to catch Tzolis by surprise and he is quickly closed down before he can give it precisely back to Rice.

Liverpool work the ball up the left to Kerkez who pings it infield to Isak. he opens his body to spay it into the stride of Gakpo who drags a right-foot shot wide of the left post.

Kerkez knocks the ball out for an Arsenal throw but immediately gets one back for his side when Van Dijk bullies Havertz who was trying to shield it.

Gabriel milks the life out of a tussle with Gakpo, going down clutching his face when slapped on the chest. A great defender but a ridiculous human being.

Arsenal kick off attacking the Kop but do not retain possession from Odegaard’s forward pass and there’s some counter-thrust until Timber takes possession on the right and drives forward to give it to Odegaard who is clumsily fouled by Nyoni who catches his ankle with his studs. This is a big day for Andoni Iraola and his emerging team and it feels like the stadium has its mojo back. It’s colourfully, lively and noisy and You’ll Never Walk Alone is being sung as loudly at any point since Liverpool were crowned champions in the spring of 2025. There is a feeling amongst home supporters that they fancy this today: that, in itself, shows progress because it wasn’t the case when Nottingham Forest and Fulham were the first Premier League visitors this season.

Any problems, he says, “let’s have a sensible chat” and he reminds them that they are responsible for their teams’ conduct as the strains of You’ll Never Walk Alone die down.

And now wreaths are laid in memory of the fallen followed by the Last Post.

Liverpool in Ron Yeatsian all red, Arsenal in that hideous faded yellow and blue. The yellow on Arsenal away kits should always be bright primrose. She didn’t wear a mustard ribbon did she, in the merry month of May?

It’s not about me [being brave in picking Nyoni], it’s about Trey. In training he has shown he has the level. For us he’s very good without the ball. It’s a big challenge for him but [he is ready].

He is young but covers a lot of space. He is aggressive as well without the ball, calm in possession, good communicating with his team-mates which is good when you know how Arsenal play. You need a lot of change of marks [positions]. There have to be a lot of things done there in the middle and he has done that in other games.

The aggression we had [against Brighton, never resting] in their structures, we go again, recover, go vertical, attack the spaces in behind, win the chance battle, one v one situations. Don’t concede territory against teams like Brighton and Arsenal. We have to be as aggressive as we were in that match.

Teams like this don’t give you easy situations [to score]. We have to be good in one v one, shots from outside the box, finishes, set plays – we should be a team that is strong in set plays. You won’t get many chances against Arsenal and when you have one you’ve got to grab it.

Yes we had good results with Bournemouth against Arsenal but the strengths of my team in Liverpool are different so you have to approach it in a different way. There are things I can use [from Bournemouth] but not a lot.

Arsenal have lost three of their last four games against Bournemouth when Iraola was in charge.

We have been very close [to winning at Anfield in the last four seasons] but moments have decided those games. We have to be really precise in those moments for victory here and that has to be the case today.

Every manager has different solutions and a different approach and Andoni’s is very clear. We expect a different game to that one [last year when Arne Slot’s side won 1-0]. It is a team that is very vertical with a real capacity to create chaos from almost all situations. They’re very good in the high press with great individuals.

[On selection] We have had issues this week with ankles and other things and had to be smart how we manage the minutes today to have players for the minutes they are available for. The conditions and the context force you to make certain decisions [on Tzolis coming straight back in after a month out].

We can’t wait. This is the kind of opportunity, challenge, mission you want to come to Anfield for.

There will be a commemoration of the fallen and pledge to care for the living before the match.

Here is a question I did not think I would be asking at any stage this season: will Liverpool win the Premier League?

It would be premature to describe this Sunday’s Anfield fixture as a title duel. Arsenal are better equipped to defend their crown, while Liverpool are a work in progress.

Whatever the outcome this weekend, Arsenal will leave Merseyside as the overwhelming favourites to claim back-to-back titles. They have a six-point lead over Liverpool. Should that extend to nine, Andoni Iraola’s primary objective coming into this season will remain unchanged; qualifying for the Champions League will represent a promising start to his reign.

What makes this weekend more significant is the champions will find a different Anfield to that which ended last season in such a downbeat mood, and came into this one uncertain of what was in store.

The discussion about what is achievable for Liverpool in the coming months is evolving by the week, the team bubbling along slightly under the radar.

There are several reasons why there are those who believe Iraola’s side might push Arsenal closer than anticipated.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool, who start the game in fifth with 15 points, and Arsenal, six points in front of them in second place. Anfield, that glorious night in May 1989 excepted, has not been the happiest of hunting grounds for Arsenal and though their record there recently – three draws in the last four visits – has perked up, they have gone 13 seasons without a victory, so long ago, in fact, that Mikel Arteta was in the side that celebrated Lukas Podolski  and Santo Cazorla earning them a 2-0 win.

Having already lost within the perimeter of the historic county of Lancashire this week, when knocked out of the Carabao Cup on penalties by League Two Fleetwood Town, the champions will be keen to end that barren streak and go into the 4.30pm kick-off on the back of three successive league victories following their defeat by Brighton. Points today, one or three, will put them ahead of Manchester City at the top of the table while victory for Liverpool would allow them to overtake Chelsea and move one point behind Brighton, the team they beat last week with the kind of performance that inspired talk of a credible title campaign.

For the visitors Max Dowman is suspended after his red card at Highbury and Bukayo Saka and William Saliba are sidelined for at least another three weeks with injury. In his pre-match press conference Arteta noted concerns about Noni Madueke (ankle), Declan Rice (thigh). Riccardo Calafiori (unspecified) and Christos Tzolis who has returned to training but all are expected to be available. Andoni Iraola has ruled out Jeremie Frimpong as well as long-term casualties Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley but hopes to be able to include Dominik Szoboszlai and Victor Muñoz. Team news should come through at 3.15pm
